text.p: Following are some major events to have occurred on May 20 in history:
1564 - John Calvin, French-born Swiss theologian, died. A leader of the Protestant reformation in Geneva, he wrote "Institutes of the Christian Religion" - a manual of Protestant theology.

1679 - The English parliament passed the Habeas Corpus Act, protecting citizens against false arrest and imprisonment. The main principles of the act were later incoporated into the U.S. Constitution.
1703 - Tsar Peter the Great founded the city of St. Petersburg as Russia's new capital.
1818 - Amelia Bloomer, American women's rights campaigner, born. She invented the knee-length garment that bears her name.
1837 - "Wild Bill" Hickok, American scout and frontiersman, born as James Butler Hickok. A crack shot and the "fastest gun in the West", he helped to bring order to the frontier.
1840 - Niccolo Paganini, Italian virtuoso violinist and composer, died. He wrote six concertos for violin.
1860 - Giuseppe Garibaldi took Palermo in Sicily in his struggle to unite Italy.
1878 - Isadora Duncan, American dancer, born. Her innovative and natural movements in dance, although controversial, met with great success in Europe.
1883 - Tsar Alexander III was crowned in Moscow. He died in 1894.
1905 - In the Russo-Japanese war, Japan's fleet destroyed the Russians at the battle of Tsushima Strait. Of the Russian fleet's 45 ships, only 12 reached safety.

1910 - Robert Koch, German bacteriologist, died. Techniques he pioneered enabled him to identify the bacteria responsible for anthrax, tuberculosis and cholera. He won the Nobel Prize for Medicine in 1905.

1923 - Henry Kissinger, U.S. statesman, born as Heinz Alfred Kissinger in Fuerth, Germany. A leading architect of postwar diplomacy, he served as President Richard Nixon's National Security Adviser (1969-73) and Secretary of State under first Nixon and then Gerald Ford from 1973 to 1977. Nobel Peace Prize winner 1973.
1936 - The 80,733-ton British Cunard liner Queen Mary sailed on her maiden voyage from Southampton to New York, carrying more than 1,800 passengers.
1937 - San Francisco's Golden Gate Bridge opened and 200,000 people crossed it on its first day. It had taken four years, four months and 22 days to complete.
1941 - In World War Two, the British ships Dorsetshire, King George V and Rodney and aircraft from the carrier Ark Royal sank the German battleship Bismarck in the Atlantic.
1941 - U.S. President Franklin Roosevelt reacted to the German navy's sinking of the merchant vessel Robin Moor by declaring a state of unlimited national emergency.
1942 - Top German Nazi official Reinhard Heydrich was shot and mortally wounded in Prague. His death on June 4 triggered savage reprisals against the populations of Moravia and Bohemia.
1951 - The Chinese Communists forced the Dalai Lama, Tibet's god king, to surrender control of his region's foreign affairs and its army to Beijing.
1963 - Jomo Kenyatta was elected first prime minister of a self-governing Kenya, becoming state president on independence from Britain the following year.
1964 - Jawalharlal Nehru, Indian statesman and first prime minister of independent India, died at 74.
1974 - French President Valery Giscard d'Estaing took office, naming Jacques Chirac as prime minister.
1980 - Dr Milton Obote, deposed as Uganda's president by Idi Amin in 1971, returned home from exile. He regained the presidency, only to be overthrown again in 1985.
1993 - British Prime Minister John Major sacked Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Norman Lamont after he was blamed for a bitter two-year recession and a humiliating currency crisis.
1993 - A suspected Mafia car bomb killed five people and badly damaged an art collection in the Uffizi Gallery in Florence, Italy.

1994 - Alexander Solzhenitsyn returned to Russia to an emotional welcome after 20 years in exile. The first action of the former dissident writer on reaching Russian soil was to salute the millions who died in Soviet prison camps.

1995 - Ukraine and a consortium of Western firms signed a memorandum to plan the closure by 2000 of the Chernobyl nuclear power station, site of the world's worst nuclear accident nine years before, and to replace it with a thermal plant.
1996 - Russia signed a deal with the leader of the Chechen rebels to end fighting in the breakaway region from June 1 in what President Boris Yeltsin called an historic moment.
